# Client Report Writing Guidelines

How we write monthly reports and quarterly business reviews (QBRs) for clients. Owner: Julieta Montes (Data and Analytics). Deadlines, templates and reviewers are set in the operations manual; this guide covers what goes into a report and how to write it.

## Required report structure

Every client report follows this order:

1. Executive summary: up to 5 bullets, results first, written for the client's CEO.
2. KPI scorecard: each KPI against its target and against the previous period.
3. Performance by channel: spend, results and efficiency for each channel.
4. Tests and learnings: what we tested during the month and what we learned.
5. Insights: what the numbers mean for the client's business.
6. Next steps for the coming month.
7. Appendix: methodology notes, attribution settings and data sources.

## KPI and chart rules

- Show at most 6 KPIs in the scorecard; agree on them with the client at kickoff and keep them stable for the whole quarter.
- Every KPI shows its value, its target, the change against the previous period and, when available, the same month last year.
- Bar and column charts start the y-axis at zero; line charts may not.
- No pie charts with more than 4 slices, no 3D charts, and no dual axes unless both series use the same unit.
- Always label the currency (USD, ARS, MXN...) and use the client's number format, for example 1.250,50 in Spanish-language reports.
- Ratios carry one decimal; percentages carry no decimals unless they are below 10%.
- State the attribution window under every conversion chart.

## Tone and language

- Write in the client's language and register: "usted" for clients in Mexico, Colombia and Chile; "vos" only for Argentine and Uruguayan clients who already write that way.
- Prefer plain words to jargon and spell out every acronym the first time it appears.
- Own the results: do not blame the algorithm or the platform without evidence.
- Bad news goes in the executive summary, never buried in the appendix.

## Writing insights

An insight has three parts: what happened (the number), why it happened (the evidence) and what it means for the client (the implication). If a sentence does not pass the "so what?" test, it is an observation and belongs in the channel section. Limit each report to 3 insights, ranked by business impact.

Example: "Cost per lead on LinkedIn Ads fell 18% after we narrowed targeting to companies with more than 200 employees, so next month we can move USD 2,000 from search to LinkedIn without losing lead quality."

## Writing next steps

- Maximum 5 next steps per report.
- Each one has an owner (Acme or client), a due date and the expected impact.
- Start each with a verb: "Launch...", "Test...", "Pause...".
- Carry over open items from the previous report and mark them as done, in progress or dropped.

## Pre-send self-check

- Every number in the text matches the dashboard for the same date range.
- Client name, logo and period are correct on every page.
- Dashboard links open without asking for extra access.
- Spelling has been checked in the report's language.
